claims.text: Pt incorporation followed by rapid thermal annealing can induce L10 ordering in an FeCoNi-based alloy.
The transformation proceeds from a disordered fcc precursor to an L10-ordered tetragonal phase.
L10 ordering enhances magnetocrystalline anisotropy.
L10 ordering increases domain-wall pinning strength.
The increased anisotropy and domain-wall pinning elevate coercivity.
The initial equiatomic FeCoNi-based alloy has an fcc structure and low coercivity.
The initial FeCoNi-based alloy has high saturation magnetization.
A near-equiatomic FeCoNiMnCuPt alloy with Pt as a coequal sixth component can form the proposed L10 phase after rapid thermal annealing.
The alloy must remain single phase and retain configurational entropy of at least 1.0R during processing.
An appropriate rapid-annealing temperature and duration can produce ordering without decomposition or formation of multiple phases.
The structural mediator is a single-phase, tetragonally distorted L10 high-entropy intermetallic.
Pt promotes ordering because of its strong spin-orbit coupling.
Pt has a tendency to promote lower-symmetry structures in this alloy.
The Pt-containing, rapidly annealed alloy will have substantially higher coercivity than a soft disordered fcc FeCoNi-based baseline.
The coercivity increase may be several-fold or greater.
Disordered equiatomic FeCoNiPd or FeCoNiPt is an appropriate low-coercivity baseline.
Coercivity enhancement occurs only when Pt incorporation and annealing produce a uniform, single-phase L10 structure.
Departures from equiatomic composition or improper thermal treatment may cause multiphase structures or inadequate ordering and eliminate the coercivity enhancement.

Prior work on a closely matching FeCoNiMnCu-Pt system observed single-phase L10 ordering, high anisotropy, and an approximately three-order-of-magnitude coercivity increase after rapid thermal annealing.
The optimal Pt concentration and annealing parameters for the proposed near-equiatomic composition are not established.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes Pt as substituting for a significant fraction of an existing constituent, whereas the intervention example retains Fe, Co, Ni, Mn, and Cu and adds Pt as a coequal sixth component.
